title: If I Could Give My Younger Self 1 Piece of Investing Advice, This Is What It Would Be
detail:
If I Could Give My Younger Self 1 Piece of Investing Advice, This Is What It Would Be
Alex Carchidi, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 8, 2026 at 11:05 AM CST 5 min read
T
Trade AT&T on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

If I could give my younger self one piece of investing advice, I'd find most of the material I'd need by reviewing my first-ever investment. My first stock was Lucent Technologies, which in 1996 was spun off from AT&T, and then bought by me at age 10 with all $500 of the birthday money I had saved up from prior years. Shortly after my purchase in late 1999, it began a long decline that saw its price fall 99.2% by September 2002.

The sting of that collapse kept me away from investing for about 15 years. So here's the investing advice that I would give to my younger self if I had to do things over again -- it's one central theme, and it has three parts.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
1. Don't put all your eggs in one basket

This advice seems obvious now, but new investors still need to learn it.

Funneling all your capital into one stock means one failure can wipe out most of your portfolio. Per research conducted at Arizona State University, about 4.3% of the nearly 26,000 U.S. stocks included in the analysis accounted for nearly all of the market's wealth creation above Treasury bills from 1926 to 2016. That's an argument for owning a large and diversified basket of stocks via an index fund like the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEMKT: VOO).

The lesson extends to the types of assets you invest in, too. The traditional 60/40 stocks/bonds portfolio split is timeless because holding bonds can make up for underperformance that stocks experience under certain conditions, and vice versa. Today, adding some cryptocurrency into your portfolio is another way to diversify even beyond that.

2. Accept that some eggs won't ever hatch

If you invest in a lot of different companies, some of those investments will not play out.

According to a 2014 J.P. Morgan study, 40% of Russell 3000 index stocks from 1980 to 2014 ended up experiencing a catastrophic loss, which in this case is defined as a 70% or larger drop from the peak with little recovery afterward. In the case of my first investment, in the telecom industry, the catastrophic loss rate was 51%.

The bigger point here is psychological in nature. Expecting every one of your stock picks to work out is not reasonable, but investing requires us to be rationally hopeful each time. The truth is that failure in investing is inevitable, and vastly more common than success. Quitting after the first big failure, as I did, cost me years of compounding, and not having the proper context to process the defeat in a constructive way was especially deleterious.

title: Why AT&T Stock Slumped in October
detail:
Why AT&T Stock Slumped in October
Eric Volkman, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 8, 2026 at 1:46 AM CST 4 min read
T
SPCX
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

A large and very well-capitalized conglomerate was bulking up its telecom assets in October, and investors felt this didn't bode well for the sector's incumbents. One that got dinged by Mr. Market was AT&T (NYSE:T), which saw its share price erode by more than 14% largely due to these fears. Even the company's estimates-beating third-quarter results, published mid-month, couldn't halt this slide.

The threat from outer space

That ambitious conglomerate is none other than the Elon Musk-led space/telecom/artificial intelligence (AI) company Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ:SPCX), or SpaceX. Its current revenue powerhouse is its Starlink telecom division, and, sensibly enough, management is aiming to bolster this business.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

On Oct. 8, SpaceX announced it had signed a definitive agreement with investment firm Grain Management to acquire up to 14 megahertz of low-band wireless spectrum. The financial particulars were not disclosed. On top of that, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved the company's application for its Gen2 satellite constellation. Both position SpaceX to continue expanding into a vertically integrated consumer wireless business, building on its roots as a high-data-transmission broadband purveyor.

Two weeks later, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX was planning to secure at least 80,000 cell sites in the U.S. Citing unidentified "people familiar with the matter," the financial news agency wrote that the company was in discussions with at least one wireless infrastructure business to help it with this goal. A sprawling network of cell sites would be foundational for a company aiming to become a nationwide wireless carrier.

So it's understandable that AT&T investors (and those of fellow incumbents Verizon (NYSE:VZ) and T-Mobile (NASDAQ:TMUS)) were spooked by these developments. Mobile telephony can be a very lucrative business. Still, it isn't an easy one, and the entry of a huge and determined competitor threatens to rock the boat — at least eventually.

Don't forget the double beats

AT&T released those quarterly results on Oct. 21, and these provided some fuel for optimism.

After all, revenue rose by 5% year over year (to $32.3 billion), an impressive growth figure given that the company's business is relatively mature. Per-share net income not under generally accepted accounting principles (non-GAAP, or adjusted) also rose at a healthy rate, climbing to $0.65 from the year-ago profit of $0.54. Both headline metrics beat consensus analyst estimates: slightly under $31.7 billion on the top line and $0.60 per share for adjusted profitability.

Crown Castle Soars 31% in a Month on SpaceX's Tower Push: "We're Talking to All Parties" ©@Изображения пользователя Axel Makhalov via Canva
Key Takeaways

Crown Castle (CCI) stock surged 31% from October 2 to November 2, closing at $87.03 as SpaceX (SPCX) pursued wireless spectrum and potential tower leases.

American Tower (AMT) could benefit from SpaceX's reported plans to access at least 80,000 U.S. cell sites.

Verizon Communications (VZ), AT&T, and T-Mobile could face additional wireless competition, while tower owners may gain a new customer.

Crown Castle traded at approximately 17.8x forward AFFO in late October, below its five-year average of 18.5x, while Wall Street's $93.50 average target implied about 7% upside from November 2.

What Happened?

Crown Castle (CCI) stock surged 31% from October 2 to November 2, climbing from $66.44 to $87.03 as SpaceX's wireless expansion plans fueled expectations of additional tower leasing revenue.

On October 8, SpaceX agreed to acquire Grain Management's nationwide 800 MHz spectrum portfolio in a transaction reportedly valued at approximately $8 billion.

On October 22, Bloomberg reported that SpaceX was discussing infrastructure agreements with Crown Castle while seeking access to at least 80,000 U.S. cell sites.

Spectrum ownership alone cannot provide nationwide terrestrial wireless coverage. SpaceX would need substantial infrastructure, creating potential leasing opportunities for established tower operators.

During Crown Castle's October 21 earnings call, CEO Chris Hillabrant addressed potential leasing arrangements with SpaceX and other providers.

"You can assume that we're talking to all parties," Hillabrant said.

Although Hillabrant did not confirm a SpaceX agreement, his comments suggested Crown Castle could pursue additional leasing opportunities as SpaceX develops its network.

Crown Castle's Earnings Show Signs of Stabilization

Crown Castle's third-quarter results showed stronger profitability despite continued rental revenue pressure.

Adjusted funds from operations (AFFO) increased 11% to $1.24 per share from $1.12 a year earlier, exceeding the $1.20 consensus estimate cited in the research brief.

However, site rental revenue declined approximately 5% to $966 million from $1.01 billion, with $61 million in DISH terminations and $5 million in Sprint cancellations weighing on organic site rental billings.

Management expects 2026 to mark the low point for organic growth, while its updated full-year AFFO guidance of $4.60 per share at the midpoint suggests continued profitability despite leasing headwinds.

TIKR's October 27 consensus estimates project revenue of $4.03 billion in 2026, $4.10 billion in 2027, and $4.19 billion in 2028.

EchoStar (ECHO) shares rose 5.2% on Friday, November 6, 2026, outpacing a 0.3% gain for the S&P 500. The company issued no announcements, earnings reports or filings around the move, which came one session after the stock fell 8.8% on November 5. So what was happening in the market and among EchoStar's peers that Friday?

What Moved Stocks On November 6?

On November 6, a strong October jobs report sent Treasury yields higher, while the Nasdaq Composite index rose 1.1% that session. Industry peer Charter reported third-quarter results and launched a new operating model alongside a plan to cut costs by $2 billion. Charter also recorded another subscriber loss in its Spectrum Internet business, and its shares fell 6.2%.

EchoStar operates a differently structured business. Management said on its August 3 call that a lot of the company's value is based on SpaceX, where EchoStar holds 261.8 million shares. Beyond that stake, EchoStar runs Boost, a wireless business that lost subscribers in the second quarter, along with a traditional video business that management said continues to throw off cash. On November 2, Reuters reported that SpaceX was in talks to buy Boost Mobile or gain access to its network.

Much of the value sits in one stake. For your own money, balance beats betting on one outcome.

Did EchoStar Move With Its Peers?

No. EchoStar climbed on its own, while the XLC fund tracking the communication services sector gained 0.4%. Four of EchoStar's five peers fell, including Comcast, which dropped 2.2%. The lone peer to advance was T-Mobile US, gaining 0.9%, trailing far behind EchoStar's rise.

Where EchoStar Stock Stands Now

A one-day rise this large is not rare for EchoStar. The stock has climbed at least this much in 16 sessions over the prior 365 days. Its most recent move of this magnitude, up or down, was the decline recorded the day before.

Over the past twelve months, EchoStar stock returned 30.8%, against 9.8% for the S&P 500. On November 6 it closed well below its highest close of the past year, $141.80 on May 20, 2026, and well above its lowest, $66.93 on November 17, 2025. Over the six months since May 8, the stock lost 25.6%, while the S&P 500 was roughly flat. On sales, EchoStar trades at 2.3 times, against 3.1 times for the S&P 500.

EchoStar's next earnings report is expected later in November 2026. The figure to watch is management's estimate of what shutting down its wireless network and paying its tax liability will cost, an expense it placed at $5 billion to $7 billion on its August 3 call.

Key Takeaways

Verizon yields 6.1% and AT&T 5.2%, after SpaceX's moves into wireless sent both stocks lower in October.

Both dividends are well covered, using 52% and 44% of free cash flow over the 12 months to Sept. 30, 2026.

AT&T plans to hold its dividend at $1.11 a share, while Verizon's dividend grew 1.9% a year from fiscal 2020 to fiscal 2025.

Analysts expect free cash flow to rise at both companies in fiscal 2026, and SpaceX plans to start mobile service on its own airwaves in early 2028.

SpaceX gave telecom income investors a real scare this fall. On Oct. 9, it agreed to buy a nationwide block of low-band spectrum from Grain Management for its Starlink Mobile service. Verizon Communications (VZ:NYSE) fell nearly 9% that day, and AT&T (T:NYSE) dropped by double digits.

SpaceX kept pushing. On SpaceX's Oct. 20 earnings call, President Gwynne Shotwell said a new spectrum purchase and FCC satellite approval would help Starlink Mobile become a major US carrier.

So if you own either one for its dividend, which check is the better one to count on?

Source: TIKR and StockAnalysis, Nov. 5, 2026.

6 safe dividend stocks paying retirees 6%+ yields

There are over 100 stocks paying 6%+ annual dividends today.

But after an extensive investment review leveraging TIKR's proprietary data, we now believe only six of them are truly safe for retirees.

They're all yours for free as part of our new investment report, which you can access right here.

Verizon's growth is back

Verizon's core business is picking up speed. Mobility and broadband service revenue rose 2.9% to $23.5 billion in the third quarter of 2026 from a year earlier, and it added 406,000 postpaid phone customers.

The cash is growing too. Free cash flow rose 12.1% to $7.8 billion in the third quarter, and Verizon now expects full-year growth to approach 12%, up from its earlier 9% to 10%. Over the 12 months to Sept. 30, 2026, the dividend used a well-covered 52% of free cash flow. Analysts see 53% for fiscal 2026.

Free cash flow has covered the dividend every year since fiscal 2018:

Verizon Communications (VZ): free cash flow vs. common dividends paid, $ billions, fiscal 2016–2025 (TIKR)

(The tightest year since then was fiscal 2022, at 77%.)

TIKR's figures show 19 straight fiscal years of higher dividends per share, though the raises are small: from $2.48 a share in fiscal 2020 to $2.73 in fiscal 2025. On its third-quarter call, management said, "We remain committed to growing the dividend and delivering enhanced returns to our shareholders through share repurchases." A 53% forward payout leaves room to keep that promise.

The main risk is SpaceX. A fourth national carrier would go straight after the wireless cash that pays this dividend.

title: Is AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) Undervalued As AT&T Tests Direct To Device Satellite Handoff?

Is AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) Undervalued As AT&T Tests Direct To Device Satellite Handoff?
Bailey Pemberton

ASTS
T
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

AT&T's recent test with AST SpaceMobile (ASTS) produced what it calls the first successful handoff between a terrestrial cellular network and a direct to device satellite connection using standard smartphones.

For investors watching AST SpaceMobile, the story right now is sharp volatility. The share price has dropped 15.22% over the last day and 52.15% over the past month, even as the 3 year total shareholder return of 631.23% points to a very large move over a longer horizon. This suggests that recent selling reflects changing views on execution risk and capital needs, despite high interest in the business model.

Compare this kind of high-volatility space story with a curated basket of other ambitious plays using the 21 high quality undiscovered gems to see what else the market is pricing for significant execution risks and opportunities.

AST SpaceMobile has already delivered a huge multi year move, then given a big chunk back in weeks. Is the real upside still in front of you, or already mostly cashed in by early believers?

Most Popular Narrative: 82% Undervalued

According to the most followed narrative on AST SpaceMobile, a fair value of $170 per share sits well above the last close of $30.20, which sets a very wide valuation gap for investors to think through.

The bull case is that AST is transitioning from technology demonstration to commercial rollout. The company reported Q1 2026 revenue of $14.7 million, reiterated 2026 revenue guidance of $150 to $200 million, and expects revenue to build sequentially through the year from gateway sales, government work, consulting, and potentially initial commercial service revenue.

See why 94 investors see AST SpaceMobile as 82% undervalued.

According to HedgeY, the narrative anchors on AST SpaceMobile moving from proofs and testing into a deployment phase with around 45 BlueBird satellites targeted in orbit by the end of 2026, carrier agreements already signed, and a capital base that was reported at roughly $3.5b in cash as of March 31, 2026. That combination feeds into an optimistic fair value estimate of $170 per share, which implies a very large gap to the current share price and underpins the 82.2% discount figure attached to the story.

The same storyline also highlights the tension here. The business is still loss making, losses have been widening over the past five years at about 59.6% per year, and ASTS is currently unprofitable with a negative return on equity of 33.83%. Analysts referenced in the statements expect earnings to grow 53.9% per year and forecast a move into profitability within three years, yet those are projections that need to be weighed against execution risk on manufacturing, launches, and commercial uptake.
